lesson.title: From Substance to Object: Scaling Up to Heat Capacity
lesson.summary: Heat capacity is the total amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a specific object by one degree Celsius, combining a substance's specific heat capacity with the actual mass of that particular object.
lesson.body:
Specific heat capacity describes a substance in the abstract, one gram of it, regardless of how much you actually have. But in the lab, and in real objects like a specific calorimeter or a particular block of metal, you usually care about the whole object in front of you, not a hypothetical single gram. That is exactly what heat capacity, symbolized C with a capital letter, describes. Heat capacity is defined as C = m c, the mass of the specific object multiplied by its specific heat capacity, with units of joules per degree Celsius, J/degree C. Unlike specific heat capacity, heat capacity is an extensive property. It depends on how much material you actually have, so a large object made of a given substance has a larger heat capacity than a small object made of the same substance, even though both share the same c value.

Once you know the heat capacity of a specific object, the heat equation simplifies to q = C delta T, since the mass and specific heat capacity are already folded into C. This version of the formula is especially useful when you are working repeatedly with the same physical object, such as a particular calorimeter, rather than starting from scratch with mass and specific heat capacity every time.

For example, take a 500.0 g block of iron, whose specific heat capacity is c = 0.449 J/(g times degree C). Its heat capacity is C = m c = (500.0 g)(0.449 J/(g times degree C)) = 224.5 J/degree C. That single number, 224.5 J per degree C, now describes this specific iron block completely: it tells you exactly how much energy this block absorbs or releases for every one degree Celsius change in its temperature. If this same block is heated so that its temperature rises by 15.0 degrees C, the heat absorbed is q = C delta T = (224.5 J/degree C)(15.0 degrees C) = 3,367.5 J, or 3.37 kJ.

This distinction between an intensive property (specific heat capacity, per gram) and an extensive property (heat capacity, per whole object) matters enormously once you start building actual calorimeters. A real calorimeter is not just the sample and the water inside it. The container itself, the thermometer, and the stirrer all have their own heat capacity, and a careful calorimetry experiment must account for the calorimeter's own heat capacity alongside the substances being studied. You will see this idea again directly when a bomb calorimeter's entire heat capacity is calibrated as one combined number, used exactly the way C was used here.
